title: Beast Games
synopsis: A thousand contestants. Millions in prize money. Cameras everywhere. You are contestant #482 and you have made it to the final ten. Don't look at the drones. Or do.

nodes.text: The arena is half stadium, half airport hangar — you can hear the air handlers running under the crowd track they're piping in. Nine circles of gaffer tape on the concrete, nine people standing on them, and you on the tenth. A producer in a navy polo explains the next round in the flat voice of a man who has watched four hundred people cry this month. A drone drifts in and holds.

choices.text: Listen carefully — strategy starts at the rules
choices.consequence: You lock onto his mouth and stop hearing the crowd track entirely. Somewhere in that phrasing there is a trapdoor, and you intend to find it first.

choices.text: Scan the other nine
choices.consequence: You stop listening at 'the next round' and start reading shoulders. Two people are already looking at you exactly the way you are looking at them.

nodes.text: Two go home each round. The eliminated get a flat payout — enough to be life-changing for about eleven days. Everyone still standing splits a pot that swells with every empty circle. The producer runs through it twice, patient, generous with detail. Then he adds, with the timing of a man who has rehearsed it, 'Except this round.' Nobody asks. The drone rotates toward the silence.

choices.text: Ask what 'except this round' means
choices.consequence: Your voice is the first one on the tape, which means it lands in the trailer. He answers you with a warm smile and no information whatsoever.

choices.text: Don't react — pretend you expected it
choices.consequence: You keep your face flat and your hands loose. Two contestants glance over to see how frightened they should be, and calibrate downward. You commit to don't react — pretend you expected it. It buys momentum toward Producer's Whisper and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

nodes.text: You take inventory. Marisol counts things under her breath — exits, crates, seconds. Devon watches faces instead of the game and gets to the answer faster. And there is Brad, who has introduced himself twice at volume and called a producer 'chief,' and who was cast for precisely that. Somewhere behind the scaffolding a story producer has a whiteboard with all four of your names on it.

choices.text: Form a quiet pact with Marisol and Devon
choices.consequence: Three words at the water station and it is done. No handshake, no eye contact, nothing a camera can later cut into a betrayal montage. You choose to form a quiet pact with Marisol and Devon. By The Stack Round, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

choices.text: Befriend Brad first; use his chaos
choices.consequence: Brad gives you his entire life in four minutes. You now own a loud, unstable asset that points wherever you last aimed it. You commit to befriend Brad first; use his chaos. It buys momentum toward Producer's Whisper and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

nodes.text: Soda crates, waist-high pallets of them, one rule: highest tower still standing at the horn. You are eleven crates in before you spot the sabotage — two players were handed crates with warped bases that rock a half inch under load. Yours sit square. Marisol's do not. She is already three levels up and has not looked down, and the horn is four minutes out.

choices.text: Win the round cleanly
choices.consequence: You build fast and honest and take it by two crates. Marisol's tower folds at the horn and she smiles at you like she means it. You win the round cleanly. The route to The Maze opens fast, while the margin for a second attempt disappears.

choices.text: Help Marisol's stack secretly while building yours
choices.consequence: You shim her base with a crushed can while pretending to steady your own. Camera four caught your hand. You will not learn that for six weeks.

nodes.text: Between setups a producer walks you behind the lighting truck, where the mics supposedly are not. He would like thirty seconds of you losing your temper at Brad. Nothing scripted — just honest feeling, aimed. In exchange, a small advantage next round. He says 'small' twice. And there it is: this is not a competition with a story attached. It is a story with a competition attached.

choices.text: Refuse the producer's offer
choices.consequence: You say no, politely, twice. He shrugs and walks toward the next contestant, and you spend the whole round wondering which of them said yes.

choices.text: Take the advantage and overact mildly
choices.consequence: You give him nine seconds of theatre and despise every one of them. The advantage turns out to be a head start you did not need. You take the advantage and overact mildly. The route to The Sponsor opens fast, while the margin for a second attempt disappears.

nodes.text: The maze is two storeys of raw plywood and it smells like a lumber yard. Cameras at every corner, and they track — you can hear the servos turning to follow you specifically. Painted arrows mark the sanctioned route. Devon falls into step beside you and tips his chin at a door with no paint on it at all, set flush into the wall like a mistake nobody bothered to fix.

choices.text: Take the unmarked door
choices.consequence: It opens onto a service corridor, cable runs, and a crew member eating a sandwich who does not look up. You come out four turns ahead. You commit to take the unmarked door. It buys momentum toward Final Six and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

choices.text: Take the marked path and stay legible
choices.consequence: You follow the arrows and stay legible the entire way. It costs you ninety seconds and buys you a floor producer who starts telling you things.

nodes.text: Round break, and a woman with a lanyard and two cases of an energy drink called VOLTIC finds you specifically. Thirty seconds, your feed, your words, and they will boost it everywhere. You run the arithmetic while she talks: three episodes in, you have become something worth renting. The can is warm in your hand. It tastes like a blue raspberry that has never existed in nature.

choices.text: Do the clip authentically
choices.consequence: You film it straight — one take, honest, mildly rude about the flavour. It clears four hundred thousand views and VOLTIC asks for another by morning.

choices.text: Politely decline; protect your image
choices.consequence: You decline and she is gone in eleven seconds. That night your name is missing from the sponsor tag, and you feel the temperature in the room change.

nodes.text: Six left. The producers have started using full legal names over the loudspeaker, which is how you learn Brad is a Bradley Duquesne and that this has stopped being a game show. The next round is called TRUST — one word, white on black, held on the wall screen four seconds longer than it needs to be. Nobody in the holding room is sitting down.

choices.text: Trust Marisol publicly
choices.consequence: You say her name out loud on camera and she goes still for a second before nodding. You have handed her a weapon and taken on a debt. You commit to trust Marisol publicly. It buys momentum toward The Charity Twist and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

choices.text: Trust nobody, smile at everyone
choices.consequence: You give everyone the same warm nothing. It works perfectly. By dinner nobody has approached you, including the two people who should have. You choose to trust nobody, smile at everyone. By The Reality of Brad, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

nodes.text: You catch Brad crouched by the cooler with a foil blister pack, thumbing a tablet into somebody's marked water bottle. He grins up at you like it is a bit you are both in on. Twelve feet behind him a camera operator has already reframed, tight on Brad's hands, and the floor producer has not said a word. Nobody here is going to stop this. They are going to air it.

choices.text: Pour the bottle out before someone drinks it
choices.consequence: You empty it into the gravel and refill from the tap. Brad watches you do it and something in his face drops clean out of character. You pour the bottle out before someone drinks it. The route to The Charity Twist opens fast, while the margin for a second attempt disappears.

choices.text: Tell production and let them handle it
choices.consequence: You report it. They thank you warmly and do nothing for two hours. The clip airs in episode nine with your name spelled wrong in the caption.

nodes.text: New card, new rule. Each of you names a charity, and a slice of whatever you walk out with goes to it — announced live, posted on the board beside your face. Marisol picks a burn unit in Sacramento without hesitating. Devon takes ninety seconds. Then the producer holds the marker out to you, and every strategy you have built acquires, in one move, a public conscience.

choices.text: Pick a charity you actually care about
choices.consequence: You name the clinic that took your mother in when nobody else would. Saying it aloud on a soundstage nearly takes your legs out from under you.

choices.text: Pick a charity that polls well
choices.consequence: You name the one with the best-known logo and the softest edges. It tests beautifully in the room and sits badly in your chest all night. You choose to pick a charity that polls well. By The Press, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

nodes.text: You find Brad behind the generator trailer with his hands on his knees, not performing for anybody. Forty-one thousand in debt, he says, and 'the loud guy' was the only character he could think of that agents actually remember. His hands will not stay still. With the volume gone, what is underneath is a man who did the math on his own life and got it wrong.

choices.text: Help Brad through it
choices.consequence: You sit down on the gravel until his breathing evens out, and neither of you says anything useful. He never runs a bit at you again. You commit to help Brad through it. It buys momentum toward Final Four and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

choices.text: Be polite but stay focused
choices.consequence: You put a hand on his shoulder, say eleven kind words, and go back inside. He is still out there when the horn sounds. You choose to be polite but stay focused. By The Press, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

nodes.text: Four circles left on the concrete. Marisol. Devon. You. And Brad, who the producers would have written in if he had not shown up on his own. The board updates and the pot crosses into a number that pays off a house, a degree, a decade of somebody's bad luck. You watch three people read it at the same moment and see precisely how badly each of them wants it.

choices.text: Honor the pact with Marisol and Devon
choices.consequence: You confirm the pact with a look and hold it. Whatever happens from here, you will be able to watch the episode with your family in the room.

choices.text: Break the pact at the right moment
choices.consequence: You begin choosing your moment — not now, not yet, but soon — and something goes quiet in you that will not come back for a long while. You break the pact at the right moment. The route to The Math opens fast, while the margin for a second attempt disappears.

nodes.text: In the gap between rounds someone from a trade site gets your number and wants a comment on footage the show is 'considering releasing.' You, off-mic, saying something about Brad you do not remember saying. They read it back to you. It is yours. It is out of context and also entirely accurate, which is worse. The piece goes up in four hours either way.

choices.text: Give a careful, kind quote
choices.consequence: You give them nineteen words that are true, generous and impossible to cut badly. It runs as the headline with the clip playing underneath it.

choices.text: Decline entirely
choices.consequence: You decline and the story runs without you, which reads on the page as guilt. Your mother calls at midnight to ask whether you are all right.

nodes.text: A steel beam nine inches wide, forty pounds of sand in a canvas bag, and no clock displayed anywhere on purpose. Ninety minutes in, your shoulders have gone from burning to numb to a distant electrical hum. Devon is beside you and his left hand has started to tremble in a way he cannot hide and cannot stop. He turns his head toward you. Two minutes, maybe, to decide.

choices.text: Wait him out
choices.consequence: You hold, and hold, and he goes down at a hundred and four minutes, hard, onto his knees. You keep standing, because dropping now would insult him.

choices.text: Take the dive for him
choices.consequence: You let the bag slide before he has to fail on camera. He knows exactly what you did, and he will never once say thank you. You commit to take the dive for him. It buys momentum toward The Solo Path and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

nodes.text: You do the arithmetic on a napkin in the holding room and then tear the napkin up, because everything in here is filmed. Split with Marisol: comfortable, clean, a good year. Break and win alone: a different life entirely. Break and lose: the appearance fee, four figures, and a story you would have to tell at parties forever. One round to pick which one you can live inside.

choices.text: Stick with the pact
choices.consequence: You choose the smaller number and feel your pulse drop for the first time in nine days. Marisol never learns you ran the math at all. You stick with the pact. The route to Final Two opens fast, while the margin for a second attempt disappears.

choices.text: Break and run for solo win
choices.consequence: You commit to breaking it, and immediately start being warmer to her. That is the part you will remember later, on the nights you cannot sleep.

nodes.text: Two circles. The lights drop to a single hard cone and the score swells like somebody's wedding. The audience is on its feet, the host has the card in his hand, and he is enjoying the pause more than is decent. Marisol's palm finds yours and squeezes once — not a signal, just a person holding onto a person. The host says your full name. Then hers.

choices.text: Propose splitting the pot live on air
choices.consequence: You say it into a live microphone before anybody can stop you, and eleven thousand people hear the producers fail to answer for four entire seconds.

choices.text: Play the final game for the win
choices.consequence: You let go of her hand and step to your mark. She nods once. The game starts, and there is no version of this where you both win. You choose to play the final game for the win. By The Win, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

nodes.text: You go alone. Marisol is gracious on camera, generous even, and in the twelve seconds after the red light dies she looks at you and files something away permanently. You win the last game by a margin nobody will remember. The check is enormous and made of foam board and weighs less than a chair. On the flight home nobody in your row speaks, and the money is already in escrow.

choices.text: Pay Marisol something off the books
choices.consequence: You wire her a figure you picked at three in the morning. She accepts it without comment and does not follow you back anywhere. You commit to pay Marisol something off the books. It buys momentum toward Live Split and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

choices.text: Move on — it's a game
choices.consequence: You decide it was a game with rules everyone agreed to. That holds up beautifully until the reunion special seats you two chairs from her. You commit to move on — it's a game. It buys momentum toward The Win and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

nodes.text: You say it live: split, evenly, both names. The host's face does something the edit will never show — half a second of real panic while he waits on his earpiece. Marisol says yes before the earpiece answers. The room comes apart. Somewhere upstairs a producer works out that this is better television than either of you winning alone, and the lawyers are told to get out of the way.

choices.text: Use your platform after the show for the charity
choices.consequence: You point every interview back at the burn unit until the questions stop being about you at all. Donations clear a million by March. You choose to use your platform after the show for the charity. By The Charity Year, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

choices.text: Use your platform for your own next thing
choices.consequence: You take the audience with you instead — a channel, a pitch deck, a name people already know how to spell. It feels like momentum, and it is.

nodes.text: You win. Confetti in your collar, in your mouth, still drifting down twenty minutes later while crew sweep it into gray drifts against the barriers. The check is six feet tall and weighs nothing at all. Your knees pick the exact moment the cameras cut to stop working, and you sit down on the concrete. Marisol reaches you before anyone else and hugs you like the last eleven days never happened.

choices.text: Share the win with the people who got you there
choices.consequence: You start a list in your phone that night — six names, then nine — before the confetti has even been swept off the floor. You choose to share the win with the people who got you there. By The Wire Transfer, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

choices.text: Take the win quietly and disappear for a year
choices.consequence: You stop answering the group chat somewhere over Nevada and let the silence build a room quiet enough to think in. You commit to take the win quietly and disappear for a year. It buys momentum toward The Wire Transfer and spends the last protection hesitation gave you.

nodes.text: A beige conference room in Century City. Two lawyers, a laptop turned toward you, a field waiting for a routing number, and a plate of pastries nobody is going to touch. The cursor blinks in the amount box. Whatever you type here becomes the version of you that exists from now on, and everyone at this table has watched somebody type it wrong before.

choices.text: Cut checks to the people who got you here
choices.consequence: You start reading names off your phone and the junior lawyer stops smirking around the fourth one. It takes fifty minutes and you enjoy all of them.

choices.text: Send one to your mother and disappear for a year
choices.consequence: One transfer, one number, and you close the laptop mid-sentence. The lawyers look at each other. You are on a northbound bus by six. You choose to send one to your mother and disappear for a year. By The Quiet Year, everyone watching will understand exactly which risk you accepted.

nodes.text: You spend the year in the passenger seat of somebody else's van, working the burn unit's fundraisers, learning the names of nurses in four states. The money goes exactly where you said it would, audited and boring and enormous. Your follower count slides back down to the number it started at, and you find you sleep better without watching it move. In December you write the producers a letter that thanks them honestly and is, unmistakably, a goodbye.

You build something smaller and stranger — six people, one room, nobody eliminated, a budget that would embarrass a Beast Games catering line. Season one does fine. Season two does well. Season three has a waiting list eight hundred names long. Two years on, a Beast producer you never much liked puts your name in front of a network unprompted, because the format works and because he watched you split a pot on live television and never quite got over it.

You write checks. Marisol, who says nothing and cashes it. Devon, who calls. Brad, who cries on the phone for four minutes and then apologizes for four more. You pay off your mother's house in a single wire and she has to sit down on the porch step. Then you set aside a fund for kids who reached final casting and got cut — small grants, no cameras, no application video. It lands like winning a second time.

You send your mother a number that ends her mortgage, and then you are gone. Twelve months of trail miles, cheap motels, and paperback novels with no takeaways in them. You gain nine pounds and lose the flinch you had developed around drones. When you come back you are a person who won a thing once, the way somebody once ran a marathon. Not contestant #482. Not a story arc. Just you, at normal volume.
